pass_a_gloss: [...] altar? Then do the Spirit-bearers say opposite things to one another? What then do we say toward these things? To him, having driven on into old age by now, quite unexpectedly the God of the whole was promising a son; and he kept saying that the seed from him would come to be vying with the unnumbered multitude of the stars; and he, since he honoured the one promising as able to set all things right, through this bearing witness to God, has been justified before him, and was carrying off, as a prize equal in worth to so God-loving a judgment, the amnesty of the ancient charges. However, God made at the proper times the oracle concerning Isaac an exercise for the righteous man; but he was in this too faithful and God-loving, as having placed nothing before the love toward God. However, just as the disciple of the Saviour says: Faith was working with the works, and from the works faith was made firm. And somewhere the marvellous Paul himself also said about the forefather Abraham: By faith he has brought Isaac, being tested, and the one who had received the promises was bringing the only-begotten, toward whom it was spoken: In Isaac seed will be called for you; having reckoned that God is able to raise even from dead. Therefore, even if it should perhaps be said that he has been justified from works because of bringing Isaac when being tested, yet this too was for him a clear demonstration of the most settled faith. And not only, but also boasting in God. Our Lord Jesus Christ, making clear the truly admirable love of the God and Father which he displayed toward us, was bringing forward for demonstration the end of the economy with flesh and the suffering upon the cross, saying somehow thus: For so God loved the world that he gave his son the only-begotten, so that everyone believing into him may not perish, but may have life eternal. For he gave truly on behalf of us his own son; and we have been ransomed, we have been released from death and sin; for not for the sake of any other thing did the Word become flesh and tent among us, than that, having endured the death of the flesh, he might lead rulers and authorities in triumph, and make idle also him who has the might of death, that is, Satan; and that he might take away the corruption, and remove together with it also the sin that played the tyrant against us; and might thus render without effect from now on that ancient curse which the nature of man underwent in Adam, as in a firstfruit of the race and as in the first root. pass_b_english: …altar?” (James 2:21). Do the Spirit-bearing writers, then, say things contrary to one another? What, then, do we say to this? To him, when he was already far on in years, the God of all promised a son, quite beyond all expectation, and said that the offspring to come from him would rival the countless multitude of the stars (Genesis 15:5). And because he honored the one who promised, bearing witness to God by this that he can accomplish all things, he was justified before him (Genesis 15:6), and received, as a reward worthy of so God-loving a mind, the forgetting of his former offences. In due course God made the oracle concerning Isaac a trial for the righteous man (Genesis 22:1–2); but in this too he was faithful and loved God, as one who put nothing ahead of his love for God. Yet, as the Savior's disciple says, “Faith was working together with the works, and by the works faith was made firm” (James 2:22). And the admirable Paul himself said somewhere of our forefather Abraham: “By faith he offered up Isaac when he was tested; he who had received the promises was offering up his only son, he to whom it was said, ‘Through Isaac shall your offspring be named’; for he reasoned that God is able even to raise from the dead” (Hebrews 11:17–19). So even if it should perhaps be said that he was justified by works because, when tested, he offered up Isaac, this too was for him a clear proof of the firmest faith.

“Not only that, but we also boast in God” (Romans 5:11). Our Lord Jesus Christ, making plain the truly admirable love of God the Father which he showed toward us, brought forward as proof the goal of his work in the flesh and his suffering on the cross, saying somewhere: “For God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son, so that everyone who believes in him should not perish but have eternal life” (John 3:16). For he truly gave his own Son for us; and we have been redeemed, set free from death and sin. For the Word “became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14) for no other reason than this: that by enduring the death of the flesh he might triumph over the rulers and authorities (Colossians 2:15) and destroy “the one who has the power of death, that is,” Satan (Hebrews 2:14); that he might do away with corruption and, with it, remove the sin that had tyrannized over us; and that he might thus make powerless from then on that ancient curse which human nature underwent in Adam, as in the firstfruits of the race and as in its first root. For Adam, by transgressing the commandment, offended his Creator; that is why he became both accursed and subject to death. But the Master of all took pity again on those who were utterly lost. For the Son came down from heaven, forgiving offences, justifying the ungodly by faith (Romans 4:5), and, as God, reforging human nature into incorruption and bringing it back to what it was in the beginning. review_notes: Old draft omitted the whole first half of the source (the James/Paul harmony on Abraham: Genesis 15:5-6, the Isaac trial, James 2:21-22, Hebrews 11:17-19, and Cyril's conclusion), dropped the Romans 5:11 lemma, translated the redemption passage twice over (paragraphs 1-6 repeated as 7-8), and inverted doctrine at 'κατηλέησε … ὁ τῶν ὅλων δεσπότης' ('brought destruction upon those utterly lost' where Greek says the Master of all took pity on them). It also misread 'ὡς ἐν ῥίζῃ τῇ πρώτῃ' as 'the root of the first' and had no citations for John 1:14, Colossians 2:15, Hebrews 2:14, Romans 4:5. Retranslated clause by clause; the Abraham sentence keeps the dative recipient (εἰς γῆρας ἐληλακότι … αὐτῷ) without a dangling clause. Both edges marked with ellipses. Old translator_notes describe the discarded draft and should be dropped.
Opens mid-sentence, completing the James 2:21 quotation begun at the end of u01-rem-mid.
